content: For each ear, there is a structure called the eustachian tube that connects the middle ear to the back of the throat. This tube is responsible for draining fluid that is naturally produced in the middle ear. If the eustachian tube becomes obstructed, fluid can accumulate in the middle ear. This stagnant fluid creates an environment where bacteria and viruses can grow, leading to an infection. Ear infections are particularly common in infants and young children because their eustachian tubes are more prone to becoming blocked. While ear infections can also occur in adults, they are less frequent compared to children. The most common bacterial pathogens responsible for otitis media are Streptococcus pneumoniae and nontypable Haemophilus influenzae. Dysfunction of the eustachian tube impairs the clearance of bacteria from the middle ear, increasing the risk of infection. In older adolescents and young adults, Haemophilus influenzae was historically a leading cause of ear infections during childhood. However, the impact of the anti-Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine on the patterns of ear infections remains uncertain, as this vaccine targets only serotype b strains, which are rarely implicated in otitis media. In addition to Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, the common cold is another significant contributor to otitis media. Colds indirectly lead to ear infections by damaging the normal protective mechanisms of the epithelial cells lining the upper respiratory tract. Another frequent bacterial cause of otitis media is Moraxella catarrhalis, a gram-negative, aerobic, oxidase-positive diplococcus. Less commonly, Mycobacterium tuberculosis can also cause otitis media. Any condition that causes swelling or blockage of the eustachian tubes can result in fluid buildup in the middle ear, increasing the risk of infection. Ear infections are most commonly observed during the winter months. While ear infections themselves are not contagious, the colds that often precede them can spread among children, potentially leading to ear infections in some. Certain medications are associated with side effects that may include ear-related issues. These drugs include: Cidofovir Moxifloxacin ophthalmic Secukinumab
